The US needs to stop treating Iran as if it is governed by "mad mullahs" and engage in dialogue with the Islamic Republic, which is emerging "stronger but different" from the US-Israeli war, a senior Iraqi Kurdish official said on Thursday.
"Iranians are often misunderstood in the West. This notion of mad mullahs is far from the truth," Bafel Talabani said at a Strategic Forum in the Iraqi Kurdistan city of Sulaymaniyah.
"We don't find it difficult talking to the Iranians," he said. "As an ally of Mr Trump and, strangely, an ally of the Iranians [I say] the mighty US can do it," he added.
Talabani leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which is the dominant political party in southeastern Iraqi Kurdistan.
The PUK's administrative zone accounts for most of the region's long border with Iran.
The PUK has historically enjoyed close ties to Tehran, but that relationship came under strain earlier this year after US President Donald Trump and his advisers tried to recruit Talabani and other Kurdish leaders to support a Kurdish insurgency in Iran.
Talabani eventually decided not to intervene.

Tehran has been pressuring Iraqi Kurdistan to clamp down on Iranian Kurdish opposition groups. In a meeting in September with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Talabani promised not to allow Iraqi Kurdistan to become "a haven for harming or threatening" the Islamic Republic.

Fighting between the kingdom and the Iran-aligned Yemeni group has intensified since July, shattering a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.

Saudi Arabia faces liquidity crunch even as oil exports rebound to pre-war levels
Saudi Arabia is feeling the pinch of a liquidity crisis as bank deposits slow and the economy comes under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, a new report from Bank of America says.
In a note to clients, Bank of America said Saudi Arabia is grappling with “contagion” caused by liquidity tightness in the UAE and a rapid slowdown in the kingdom’s own economy, according to an article published on Bloomberg on Tuesday.
The report said Saudi banks are feeling the pain in the UAE, which is also grappling with fallout from the Iran war and tighter liquidity. Saudi banks are closely linked to their Emirati neighbours, with a high number of interbank transactions contributing to deposits at Saudi banks.
At the same time, the Saudi economy is under strain and government entities are making withdrawals from Saudi banks. But loan demand is high, which is effectively raising the cost of Saudi money.
The liquidity strain is notable for Saudi Arabia because its currency is directly pegged to the US dollar, along with Gulf states including the UAE, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain.

El-Quseir is pitch black at night. The only light inside this decaying labyrinth of a port comes when a battered Bajaj motorcycle purrs down the odd alley, casting a headlight on one of the town’s many stray dogs, or a passerby flashes a phone, lighting up a decaying wooden balcony.
The old mayor’s house is easy to find in the darkness. It emits a warm, golden light. When I arrive, a crowd is already gathered on the colonnaded veranda; some men in djellabas, others in the uniform skinny jeans of the Middle East.
I spot the odd Cairo hipster among them. The women attendees are especially radiant in make-up. Why shouldn’t they be.
Tonight is a Hazz night, the name, which in Arabic means luck, given to soirees down Egypt’s Red Sea coast, where the simsimiyya , a triangular lyre, is played to ballads about old ports, friendships and legendary seafarers.
The simsimiyya looms large over El-Quseir.
“The men here would be at sea for four months at a time. They would save a spot on their dhow just for a simsimiyya player to entertain them,” Aly El-Sayed, the founder of Bahar, a community organisation working to preserve the city's heritage and marine ecosystem, told me.
Aly is the host of tonight’s gathering. The old mayor’s house, a butter-yellow bungalow built in 1888, has been repurposed as Bahar’s home.
“We tried not to change much. We were even careful not to paint too much,” El-Sayed said.
'They sang all the time'
I knew that music was central to life aboard dhows, traditional wooden sailing boats, that plied goods, including slaves, between East Africa and Arabia up until the mid-20th century.

His comments set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders at the UN conference on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, Reuters reported.
Guterres pointed to rising carbon emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters in his speech.
“But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs.”
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.
The summit opened on Monday and has, relative to its importance, received little attention against a backdrop of numerous wars, rampant inflation and other crises.

Analysis: The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
ne of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
The trauma of the Hamas-led 7 October attack may have bypassed the Haredi spiritual leadership and its veteran MPs, but the wider Haredi public, including the generally more conservative Lithuanian community, understands that something momentous has happened in Israel. This is particularly true of the younger generation.

He told Mike Rogers, the Republican he had just beaten, "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope." Then he turned to those who call people hateful for believing that Palestinian children should not be killed with American tax dollars: "That's not hate. It's love."

The GCC body representing six Gulf states established a joint defence agreement in 2000, stating that an attack on one member is an attack on all.
The GCC’s commitment to self-defence, however, is not as ironclad as that of the Nato military alliance.

Israel's parliament sworn in as Eisenkot tries to forge a government
Israel's parliament was sworn in on Tuesday without a new government, after a deadlocked general election stripped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of his parliamentary majority but left his main rivals with nuclear path to power.
Lawmakers elected in the 27 October vote took their oaths of office as Gadi Eisenkot, a former general, sought to forge a coalition after Israel's president ask him on Sunday with forming a government.
Eisenkot and his allies also lack a majority and he has yet to strike deals with parties that could bring him to power. If both Eisenkot and Netanyahu fail to form coalitions, another election could follow.
Presiding over the swearing-in ceremony, President Isaac Herzog told lawmakers: "You must do everything to avoid a repeat election."
"Reach out a hand for compromise, even between rivals... Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability and experience found in every part of this House."

Ashraf Ghazaly, the owner of the heavy machinery, said more than 150 settlers took part in the attack. They threw stones at Palestinian workers before storming one of the workshops and setting fire to machinery, vehicles and equipment.

The settlers came from the "Navitar" settlement, established on land belonging to Beita.
This latest attack is part of a series of repeated settler assaults on Beita’s industrial zone, which houses stone-cutting workshops, other businesses and heavy machinery that provide a vital source of income for dozens of families and workers in the town.

One of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
This social model developed in Israel, where Torah study in yeshivas and kollelim has become a central way of life and even a social ideal for Haredi men. Many devote years to religious study instead of entering the labour market or undertaking military service.
The model rests on the belief that Torah study is a supreme value and a communal obligation, supported financially by families, the community, the state and religious support networks.
For decades, the Haredi parties were among the most stable and predictable blocs in Israeli politics. The government, which the insurgents have vowed to overthrow, has managed to contain much of the fighting, although explosions were heard in Addis Ababa in October.
Tigray is no stranger to conflict. Amid accusations of war crimes and genocide, hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions more displaced during the civil war from 2020-22.
But now there are fears that the current conflict could escalate into a war between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea, which it accuses of backing the rebels. The two countries severed relations in October.
The Red Sea region is already beset with war across Sudan, Yemen and Somalia.
Ethiopia has an ally in the UAE, while Eritrea can look to Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Sudan for support.

Where is Tigray?
Tigray is Ethiopia’s northernmost state, bordering Eritrea and a small part of Sudan.
Roughly the size of Slovakia or the US state of West Virginia, it has a population of around 7.5 million people, according to the Ethiopian government.
The majority of the inhabitants are Tigrayan, one of the 80-plus ethnic groups in Ethiopia and make up around six percent of the overall population.

Senior UAE official says Gulf faces 'prolonged uncertainty' with no settlement to Iran war
A senior UAE official warned that the Gulf must be prepared for a “long period of uncertainty” in which the US and Iran are not able to come to a political settlement to end their war, leaving the region in a state of limbo.
"We should... prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic advisor to UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed, said on Monday at a forum in Abu Dhabi.
Gargash’s remarks come as the Middle East tries to decipher whether US President Donald Trump will launch fresh strikes on Iran.
Expectations of a new attack were high until last week, when on 3 November the Democrats won a sweeping midterm election victory that Trump and Vice President JD Vance attributed to the unpopularity of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Trump told CNN on Monday it was “highly unlikely” he would attack while negotiations are ongoing.

A new investigation has traced a major anti-Muslim propaganda campaign targeting Britain back to Israel.
The campaign, uncovered by academics Marc Owen Jones and Sohan Dsouza, was at its height before the UK's 2024 general election and the anti-Muslim riots that raged across the country later that year.
It involved large numbers of paid advertisements warning of an Islamic takeover of Britain masterminded by Qatar.
"Between 2024 and 2026, our investigation recorded more than 154m exposures to its British-targeted material," Jones and Dsouza wrote in an article published by The Nerve.
"Its first wave of British advertising ran in the months before the 2024 general election. The ads were also hammering the UK in the winter and spring leading up to the anti-Muslim riots that followed the Southport murders."
In July 2024, violent disorder raged in cities and towns across Britain, targeting Muslims and ethnic minorities, after the murder of three young girls in Southport by Axel Rudakubana.
